WaveLink Chat Explained

EN2130 Communication Design Project · Team WaveLink · 2026

WaveLink Chat

A WhatsApp-style chat and game center for two to four stations. Each station is one PC with one ANTSDR E200. All stations share one 4 MHz channel at 2.5 GHz: they take turns in time slots, and inside its slot a station reaches every other station at once, each on its own Gold code. This page explains how every layer is built, why each design choice beat the alternatives, how the two games work and which edge cases the system survives; a playground lets you switch stations on and off and move them around; and the last chapters cover running, testing and what is still open.

  • 2.5 GHz carrier, 4 MHz
  • 4 MS/s · 2 Mchip/s
  • 31-chip Gold codes · 14.9 dB gain
  • BPSK · QPSK · 16-QAM + 5G NR LDPC
  • TD-CDMA slots + one-hop relaying
  • up to 258 kb/s per link

1

How the project is implemented

WaveLink Chat is four layers stacked on one ANTSDR per PC. The radio work happens in a GNU Radio Companion flowgraph, grc/cdma_phy.grc, which the app compiles with grcc every time a station starts. Everything above the flowgraph is Python: a link layer that shares the air in time slots (mac.py, tdma.py), an application layer for messages, encryption, profiles and games (node.py, games/), and a web UI served from the station to the browser.

1.1 The layers, and one message's journey

What happens when Alice sends Bob a photo:

  1. BrowserAlice picks a quality on the quality sheet (480, 640, 1280 px or the original). The page re-encodes the photo as WebP on a canvas and posts it to her station.
  2. Application · node.pyThe station wraps it in an envelope (crypto byte | meta length | meta JSON | body), compresses it with zlib if that helps, and with --key seals it with AES-256-GCM, using the addresses (1, 2) as associated data.
  3. Link layer · mac.pyThe message is cut into 1,009-byte fragments (up to 65,535 of them) with a message id, gets the bulk priority, and gets the fastest modulation and code rate that Bob's last SNR report allows.
  4. Time slots · tdma.pyWhen Alice's slot comes round, her slot header goes out on the broadcast code 0 and, starting on the same chip, the photo's fragments go out on code 2, Bob's code. Each burst is handed to the flowgraph with an at tag: the exact chip it must start on.
  5. Flowgraph TXCRC-32 is appended, the LDPC Encoder adds parity, the Framer turns the bits into constellation indices behind a preamble and a Golay-coded header, lane 2 spreads every symbol with Gold code 2, the Burst Combiner puts the burst on its chip, and the RRC filter and the PlutoSDR Sink send it to the ANTSDR.
  6. Flowgraph RX at BobThe matched filter and the CDMA Despreader find the preamble on code 2, read the header, track timing and carrier, and hand the symbols to the Constellation Soft Decoder for that modulation, then the LDPC Decoder, then the CRC-32 check. Frames with a bad CRC are dropped there.
  7. Link layer at BobBob's station puts the fragments back together and acknowledges them in its next two slot headers (an ACK record: cumulative base plus a SACK bitmap and the SNR it measured). Alice resends only what is missing.
  8. Application at BobThe station decrypts, stores the photo in its history and pushes it to Bob's browser with Server-Sent Events. Alice's tick turns ✓✓, and blue when Bob opens the chat (a read receipt).
Brief requirementHow WaveLink meets it
Digital modulationDS-CDMA with 31-chip Gold codes, RRC α = 0.35. BPSK preamble and Golay-coded header; payload BPSK, QPSK or 16-QAM, with LDPC rate ½, ⅔, ¾, ⅚ or uncoded, chosen per link from the measured SNR.
Unique addressingTwice: node N listens on Gold code N (a frame for someone else is never even despread), and every frame carries a dst byte that the link layer checks.
AcknowledgementsSelective-repeat ARQ with cumulative and selective (SACK) acknowledgements, carried in the next slot headers.
CRC error detectionCRC-8 on the PHY header, CRC-32 on every frame (stock Stream CRC32 blocks in the flowgraph). Bad frames are dropped.
Packetization and reassembly1,009-byte fragments, up to 65,535 per message (≈ 66 MB; the app allows 64 MB).
Text, images, audioText with emoji; photos at a chosen size; voice notes and audio files re-encoded to Opus; any other file.
ApplicationChat (1:1 and an "Everyone" group), tic-tac-toe, and a game center with UNO and a real-time street race.
Bonus: encryption, priority, dashboardAES-256-GCM with a scrypt key; four priority classes; a radio dashboard with constellation, spectrum, slot plan, timing and links.

1.2 The physical layer: the GNU Radio flowgraph

The flowgraph has 68 processing blocks: 7 Embedded Python blocks that hold the project's own DSP, and 61 stock GNU Radio blocks for everything else (CRC, spreading, symbol mapping, filtering, soft decoding and the radio). Its variables fix the air interface: samp_rate = 4e6, sps = 2 samples per chip (so chip_rate = 2 Mchip/s), sf = 31 chips per symbol, preamble_bits = 48, max_payload = 1024 bytes and rolloff = 0.35. The Gold codes themselves are the variables code_0 … code_4, written into the file as ±1 lists.

Click any block below to see what it does and the parameters it has in cdma_phy.grc. The code lanes and the receive branches are drawn once and stacked: the real graph has five lanes (codes 0 to 4) and three branches (BPSK, QPSK, 16-QAM).

Two details make the stock blocks fit a burst system. First, a burst carries its metadata as stream tags: PDU to Tagged Stream turns the PDU's pwr (power backoff) and at (start chip) into tags on the burst's first chip, and Tagged Stream Multiply Length keeps packet_len right after Repeat ×31 has made 31 chips of every symbol. Second, the radio must never run dry, so the CDMA Burst Combiner sends zeros between bursts. The stock PDU to Stream block stops instead, which starves the PlutoSDR Sink.

tools/epy/combiner.py · CDMA Burst Combiner, general_work()for t in tags:
    if pmt.eq(t.key, self.len_key):          # one entry per complete burst on this lane
        self.lens[i].append((pmt.to_long(t.value), pwr.get(t.offset, 0.0), at.get(t.offset)))
...
# only complete bursts are scheduled, so a burst is never cut by a gap
while self.lens[i] and self.have[i] >= self.lens[i][0][0]:
    length, gain_db, start = self.lens[i].popleft()
    burst = self._take(i, length)
    self.core.push(self.codes[i], burst, gain_db, at=start)   # sum with the other codes;
                                                             # 'at' = the chip it must start on
out = output_items[0]
self.core.read_into(out)                     # zeros when no lane has anything to send

1.3 Spreading and despreading

In the transmit lane, Chunks to Symbols turns each symbol index into a constellation point, Repeat holds it for sf = 31 chips, and Multiply multiplies it chip by chip with a Vector Source that repeats the lane's Gold code. The result occupies 31 times the bandwidth of the symbols. The receiver multiplies the incoming chips by the same code and adds up the 31 products: the wanted symbol adds up coherently (×31), while noise and every other code add up like random numbers. That ratio is the processing gain, 10·log10(31) = 14.9 dB.

Try it: Alice sends four BPSK symbols to Bob on code 2 while Carol sends to Dave on code 4. Pick the code the receiver despreads with, make Carol louder (the near-far problem), or shift her code phase.

wavelink/config.py · receiver-based code assignmentBROADCAST_CODE = 0          # Gold-code index used for broadcast / beacons

def code_index_for(addr: int) -> int:
    """Receiver-based code assignment: a frame is spread with the code of the
    station it is addressed to.  Broadcasts use the common code 0."""
    if addr == BROADCAST_ADDR:
        return BROADCAST_CODE
    return addr

Codes belong to receivers. Station N despreads only code N and the broadcast code 0. That has three consequences the rest of the design relies on: a station never spends CPU on traffic for others; one transmitter can serve several stations at the same instant by summing bursts on their codes (the Burst Combiner's job); and two senders that reach the same station at once arrive at different code phases, so the receiver can track and decode both.

1.4 Bursts and frames, field by field

A message is wrapped four times on its way to the antenna, and each wrapper is there for a reason. The envelope tells the receiving app what the message is and who sent it. The link-layer frame lets the link layer address it, number it, put fragments back together and detect errors. The LDPC codeword corrects errors. The burst lets a receiver find the frame, read how it was sent and decode it, with nothing agreed in advance. Below, one short text, "Hi Bob!" from Alice to Bob, goes through every layer. The bytes are the real ones, produced with the project's own code.

The burst on the air

The CDMA PHY Framer builds every burst as a list of symbol indices into sym_table (0–1 BPSK, 2–5 QPSK, 6–21 16-QAM), so one code lane can carry any modulation and the modulation can change from one burst to the next.

PartSizeWhat it carriesWhy it is there
Preamble48 BPSK symbolsA known ±1 pattern, a different one for each Gold codeThe receiver finds the burst with it (a differential correlator that a carrier offset doesn't disturb) and takes symbol timing, carrier phase and frequency from it. Because the pattern belongs to one code, a strong burst on another code that leaks through is not mistaken for one of ours.
Header: length11 bitsBytes in the payload, CRC-32 included (at most 1,024; 11 bits would allow 2,047)Where the payload ends (bursts are padded), and with modulation and rate it fixes the LDPC codeword size, so decoding can start.
Header: modulation2 bits0 differential BPSK, 1 QPSK, 2 16-QAM, 3 coherent BPSKThe link layer picks it per frame from the receiver's SNR reports; the receiver just reads it here, so it can change with every frame.
Header: code rate3 bits0 uncoded, 1 ½, 2 ⅔, 3 ¾, 4 ⅚The same for the LDPC rate.
Header: CRC-88 bitsOver the 16 bits above (polynomial 0x07)Throws away a "header" decoded from noise or from another code's leakage before the receiver spends time on a payload.
Golay (24,12) × 248 BPSK symbolsThe 24 header bits, codedThe header has to be read before anything else, at a lower SNR than the payload: minimum distance 8, any 3 errors per codeword corrected, soft decoding to about 1 dB.
PayloadE bits as symbolsThe LDPC codeword's sent part (or the plain bits, uncoded), Gray-mappedThe link-layer frame itself.
Pad0–15 symbolsIdle symbolsMakes every burst a multiple of 16 symbols, so stock GNU Radio blocks that work in SIMD-sized chunks don't hold its last chips back until the next burst. The receiver stops at the length.

Inside the payload: the link-layer frames

Every frame starts with the same six bytes, type · flags · dst · src and a 16-bit word whose meaning depends on the type, and ends with a CRC-32 that the flowgraph's Stream CRC32 block appends before LDPC encoding and checks after decoding.

TypeBytes 4–5ThenUsed for
1 · DATAmsg_idfrag_idx (2) · frag_count (2) · fragment (≤ 1,009 B)Fragments of a reliable message
6 · FWDmsg_idrelay (1) · frag_idx (2) · frag_count (2) · fragmentA fragment going through a relay
5 · SLOTcycletx_sample (4) · nonce (2) · status · want_ms · lead · lead_seen (2) · sectionsThe TD-CDMA slot header, first in every slot
2 · ACKmsg_idfrag_count (2) · base (2) · trigger (2) · snr · SACK bitmapACKs of spread ALOHA (TD-CDMA puts them in slot headers)
3 · BEACONnn × (address, Es/N0) · JSONPresence, name, picture, key id, clock
4 · DGRAM0payloadRace car states and clock pings: sent once, never acknowledged

The flags byte holds the priority (bits 0–1), the ACK request of spread ALOHA (bit 2) and the frame's own transmit power backoff in dB (bits 3–7), so a receiver always knows how strong the path is at full power. Pick a frame below to see every field, what it holds in the example and what it is for.

What a burst costs

Every burst pays 96 symbols of preamble and header (1.49 ms) whatever it carries, and every fragment 14 bytes of MAC header, fragment fields and CRC-32. A short text is therefore mostly overhead: 7 bytes take 5.2 ms. A full 1,009-byte fragment at uncoded 16-QAM carries 243 kb/s of information while it is on the air, 94 % of the raw 258 kb/s, which is why files go in full fragments.

Why the frames look like this

  • Addressed twice. The burst is spread with the destination's Gold code, so a station never despreads frames for others; the dst byte then catches anything decoded from cross-correlation, marks broadcasts (255, on code 0) and lets a relay take FWD frames that are not its own.
  • Every frame describes itself. Modulation and code rate are in the PHY header, the transmit power in the flags. Each frame can use a different rate and power, and nothing has to be negotiated or announced.
  • CRC and numbering per fragment. msg_id, frag_idx and frag_count with a CRC-32 on every frame make selective repeat possible: only the fragments that were lost go again, and fragments may arrive in any order (directly and through a relay).
  • 1,009-byte fragments. One burst holds at most 1,024 bytes: one LDPC codeword (base graph 1 takes up to 1,056 bytes) and an 11-bit length. 4 bytes go to the CRC and 11 to the largest header, FWD's, so a fragment can be relayed unchanged.
  • A slot header made of sections. The fixed fields every station needs come first, then tag–length sections. When a slot is full the plan always goes in and the optional sections (duplicates, timing, link table, ACK records) wait for the next slot; new sections can be added without breaking old stations.
  • ACKs inside headers. With TD-CDMA a receiver needs no ACK bursts: its records ride in its next two slot headers, so no sender pauses for an ACK, and every member of a group acknowledges in its own header.
  • Datagrams for state that goes stale. A car state is useless 100 ms later, so it has no message number, no ACK and no retry, always uses the most robust rate, and only the newest one is sent.
  • Encryption inside, addresses outside. Only the envelope is encrypted. The MAC header stays readable, so relaying, ARQ and power control work without the key, while the addresses are bound into the GCM tag.

1.5 Messages of any size: texts, photos, voice notes and files

“Hi Bob!” fits into one frame. A longer text, a photo, a voice note or a file goes through the same wrappers, with three differences. The app first makes it as small as it can. The link layer then cuts the envelope into fragments of at most 1,009 bytes and puts each into a DATA frame of its own, numbered and with its own CRC-32, sent as a burst of its own. And the bursts go out a few at a time, in the sender's time slots, cycle after cycle, until the receiver's acknowledgements show that every fragment has arrived. Choose a message and follow it down: every size is worked out the way the code works it out.

Typical messages

Bob close to Alice (16-QAM uncoded), nothing else to send, no losses, times from the moment the message is queued; photo sizes are typical ones for a 12-megapixel phone photo:

A text of up to a few hundred bytes arrives within about 0.1 s, however many stations are on the air. A bigger message goes one frame per cycle at first (with three or four stations an idle slot is shorter than a full frame, so it waits instead), and once Alice's slot has grown, about 1.4 s in, three full frames per cycle: 187 kb/s with two stations, 152 kb/s with four. So a Standard photo takes about 2 s and an original 3 MB photo over two minutes. Because a four-station idle slot (22 ms) is shorter than any full frame (33.2 ms even uncoded), a text of two fragments takes 1.5 s there instead of 0.2 s (chapter 11). Compression counts for more than the rate: the 1 MB CSV goes in a quarter of the PDF's time.

The rules, whatever the size

  • The app shrinks first. Text is UTF-8, compressed with zlib level 9 when that makes it smaller (most texts longer than a line or two). Photos are scaled and re-encoded as WebP in the browser (Saver 480 px, Standard 640 px, HD 1280 px, or the original), voice notes are Opus at 12 or 24 kb/s, and neither is compressed again. A file over 2 KB is compressed with zlib level 6 only if its first 256 KB shrink below 90 % at level 1 and the whole file below 95 %. (node.py send(), media.js)
  • One envelope, one seal. The meta JSON (60–200 bytes) and the 28 bytes of AES-GCM are paid once per message, not per frame.
  • Fragments of 1,009 bytes, the last one shorter. A burst holds 1,024 bytes: 11 go to the largest header (FWD) and 4 to the CRC-32. At most 65,535 fragments, so a message holds up to 66.1 MB. Each fragment costs 14 bytes of frame and 96 symbols of preamble and header: 1.4 % and 4.5 % of a full frame, most of a short text. (mac.send)
  • One rate for every frame of a message in a slot. The link layer picks it from the receiver's SNR reports and the power it uses; a message of one or two fragments goes two rungs lower, but no lower than its slot allows; a group broadcast takes the weakest member's rate. (mac.mod_for, group_mcs, tdma._data_maker)
  • Slots of whole frames. Frames go back to back in the sender's slot, on the receiver's code, in parallel with the slot header. A sender with a backlog asks for a slot of a whole number of its frames, as close to 100 ms as possible (at most 250 ms); the lead announces the bigger slot at least 1 s ahead, so a transfer reaches its full rate about 1.4 s after it starts. (tdma._build_slot, _lead_plan_update)
  • Selective repeat from the headers. The receiver's next slot header says which fragments it has: everything below the first missing one, then a bitmap. Anything sent before the newest frame it heard and still missing goes again, first thing in the next slot. A sender keeps at most 496 fragments in flight beyond the first unacknowledged one, the span one record can describe. (mac._apply_record, inflight_ok)
  • Priorities in every slot. A slot is filled by priority, then age: urgent messages and game moves, then texts, then photos, voice notes and files. A text sent in the middle of a photo goes in Alice's next slot, ahead of the photo's remaining frames. Messages to different stations go on their own codes in the same slot, at the same time.
  • Groups and relays. A group message is one broadcast that every member acknowledges in its own header. A member the sender can only reach through a relay gets a copy of its own as FWD frames, which the relay passes on in its own slot, so every frame takes two slots. (node.py send(), tdma._fwd_maker)
  • Putting it back together. The receiver files fragments by sender and msg_id, in any order, directly or through a relay, and hands the envelope up when the last one is in; then it reads the meta and decompresses the body. A transfer cancelled at either end stops at both. (mac._on_data, node.py)

1.6 The receiver: inside the CDMA Despreader

The Despreader block hands its samples to a worker thread (DespreaderCore in grc_phy.py), so the GNU Radio scheduler never waits for Python DSP. The worker runs modem.Demodulator on batches of about 20 ms:

  1. Matched filter. The stock FFT Filter with the same RRC taps as the transmitter, in front of the Despreader.
  2. Code correlation at every sample offset, but only where a burst can start: around each other station's slot start (±0.27 ms), right after a burst just found on a code, and over the whole join slot. Every 8th cycle, and for 1.5 s after a possible timing slip, it searches everywhere. With three idle stations this cut the receiver's CPU from 3.2 to 1.2 s per second of air in the simulator.
  3. Differential preamble detector |Σ q_k c_k c*_{k−1}|, normalised by the despread energy. Comparing each symbol with the one before cancels the carrier offset, so bursts are found with up to ±16 kHz between two ANTSDR crystals. It also gives symbol timing and a coarse CFO.
  4. A second, coherent check of every detection against the known preamble in four segments rejects noise and other codes' data before any decoding.
  5. Fractional-delay despreading: each symbol is despread at a few whole-sample offsets and an 8-tap windowed-sinc filter interpolates to 1/64 of a sample. 16-QAM needs that accuracy. An early-late DLL tracks a sample-clock difference of up to 30 ppm.
  6. Header and carrier. The Golay header is decoded by soft maximum likelihood (correlation with all 4,096 codewords) and checked with CRC-8. Its 48 symbols then become known, and the CFO is re-estimated over all 96 known symbols. A decision-directed 2nd-order loop, anchored on the preamble and header, tracks the carrier through the payload.
  7. Out to the stock blocks. The symbols leave as a PDU tagged with modulation, code rate, length, SNR, CFO and the burst's receive sample index (the time slots need it). A PDU Filter on mod routes it to the matching Constellation Soft Decoder, whose soft bits go to the LDPC Decoder and the CRC32 check.

A "ghost" filter rejects sidelobes of much stronger bursts and duplicate decodes, which matters at the high SNR of a short lab link. Three seconds of pure noise on two codes gives zero detections.

1.7 LDPC and adaptive modulation and coding

Every frame is one codeword of the 5G NR LDPC code (3GPP TS 38.212, base graph 1). Its 46 × 68 base matrix is lifted by a factor Z (51 sizes from 2 to 384) to fit the frame: a 1 KB frame uses Z = 384, a 30-byte ACK Z = 11. The encoder works systematically, as 5G does. All rates are prefixes of one mother codeword (the first 2Z information bits are punctured, then the first E = K/R bits are sent), so one matrix serves ½, ⅔, ¾ and ⅚, and the 5G bit interleaver spreads each codeword across the bits of QPSK and 16-QAM symbols. The decoder is a layered normalised min-sum (α = 0.75) that stops as soon as every parity check passes: 1–3 iterations at good SNR, at most ldpc_max_iter = 20.

Each ACK carries the SNR the receiver measured, and the sender picks the fastest rung whose threshold that SNR meets (mac.MCS_TABLE). A window that loses more than 20 % of its frames drops the link one rung for 10 s. Drag the link quality:

wavelink/mac.py · the table the sender climbsMCS_TABLE = [   # (name, Es/N0 needed in dB, info bits per symbol)
    ("qpsk-1/2", 5.0, 1.0), ("qpsk-3/4", 6.0, 1.5), ("qpsk-5/6", 7.0, 1.667), ("qpsk", 15.5, 2.0),
    ("16qam-1/2", 9.5, 2.0), ("16qam-2/3", 11.0, 2.667), ("16qam-3/4", 12.5, 3.0),
    ("16qam-5/6", 14.0, 3.333), ("16qam", 22.5, 4.0),
]   # (BPSK rungs omitted here)
AUTO_LADDER = ["qpsk-1/2", "qpsk-3/4", "qpsk-5/6", "16qam-1/2", "16qam-2/3", "16qam-3/4",
               "16qam-5/6", "16qam"]

LDPC, CRC-32 and ARQ together are hybrid ARQ type I: the code corrects most errors, the CRC catches what it can't, and ARQ resends those frames. Adaptive modulation keeps that rare.

1.8 The link layer

Addressing

A frame whose dst is neither this station nor 255 (broadcast) is dropped and never acknowledged. A relay also takes FWD frames that name it. Frames from itself are dropped, except its own slot headers, which it uses to measure its timing.

Fragmentation

1,009-byte fragments, so every fragment also fits a FWD frame. A big transfer streams in every slot, up to 496 fragments beyond the first unacknowledged one.

Selective-repeat ARQ

Each receiver puts an ACK record in its next two slot headers: sender, msg_id, fragment count, cumulative base, the fragment heard last, Es/N0 and a SACK bitmap of up to 512 fragments. A fragment older than the one heard last and still missing is known lost and goes again in the sender's next slot. A timeout (3 cycles + 2 hand-over times + 0.1 s, or 2.5 × the round trip + a cycle) resends what is in flight.

Priority

Four classes: control/ACK, urgent ⚡, normal, bulk media. In a slot each code serves its messages in that order, so an urgent text overtakes a 10 MB transfer in the sender's next slot.

Group messages

One broadcast on code 0 at the rate the weakest member can take. Every member acknowledges it in its own header; the sender resends what any member misses, shows a tick count per member (2/3), and gives a silent member its own copy after 4 timeouts.

Transmit power control

Each frame carries its backoff, receivers report Es/N0 at full power, and senders back off to a target of 25.5 dB at the receiver: what uncoded 16-QAM needs (22.5 dB) plus 3 dB. Power follows the best recent report, rate follows the latest, so interference lowers the rate instead of starting a power race.

Transmit power control, step by step

StepHow
Each frame says its powerBits 3–7 of the flags byte carry the frame's backoff (0–31 dB). The receiver adds it to the Es/N0 it measures, so it knows every path at full power, whatever power was used.
Receivers reportIn every ACK record, and in the link tables of slot headers and beacons: how each station hears each other one, at full power.
Senders back offTo 25.5 dB at the receiver, what uncoded 16-QAM needs (22.5 dB) plus 3 dB, so only power the link can't use is taken away. Up at once, down in steps of 2 dB or more, at most 30 dB, and back to full power when a station's reports stop for 60 s. The modulation is then chosen for the Es/N0 the receiver will see at that power.
Power from the path, rate from the interferenceThe reports are SINR. Power follows the best recent report (which falls 0.5 dB/s), the modulation follows the latest, so a burst of interference lowers the rate instead of starting a power race between stations.
Outer loopA backed-off link that keeps losing frames although its receiver reports no interference aims 3 dB higher, up to +12 dB, and 1 dB lower per 30 s without losses: impairments the Es/N0 estimate doesn't show.
One power per slotWith TD-CDMA a slot goes at what its weakest listener needs; a station that hasn't reported yet counts as needing full power, so a newcomer hears us. With more than two codes in a slot each gets 10·log10(codes / 2) dB less, so their sum never exceeds two full-power codes (tdma._slot_bo).
In the flowgraphMAC → PHY puts pwr in the PDU metadata, the LDPC Encoder and the Framer keep it, PDU to Tagged Stream turns it into a tag on the burst's first item, and the Burst Combiner scales the burst. --tx-atten sets the ceiling.

With TD-CDMA one station transmits at a time, so power control isn't needed against near-far there: it keeps receivers from being overdriven (a neighbour arrives at about 25 dB instead of 40–50 dB) and the lab's band quieter. With spread ALOHA it is what makes the scheme work at all. On the simulated air, with Alice, Carol and Dave 24 dB closer to each other than to Bob, Bob's 40 KB to Dave failed without it while Alice sent a file to Carol, and arrived in 4.6–9.1 s with it (Alice 16–20 dB down). Where no station is much nearer than the others it costs nothing: three 150 KB files at once took 54–58 s on the GNU Radio simulation with it, 65–66 s without. A lower target such as 17 dB would protect weak neighbours more, but would put every strong link on coded modulation: slower, an LDPC decode per frame and more receiver CPU at every station.

1.9 TD-CDMA: time slots in radio samples

The stations take turns. A repeating cycle has one slot per station plus a join slot for newcomers. In its slot a station sends its slot header on the broadcast code (QPSK ½, 4.6–9.6 ms) and, starting on the same chip, its frames for each destination on that destination's code, all at one power. Nobody else transmits during the slot, so nobody is deafened by their own transmitter and no near station drowns a far one. Pick which stations have data queued:

Who leads, who joins, who takes over

The first station on the air leads: its header opens the cycle and carries the cycle number and the slot plan. A starting station listens for 1.2 s plus 0.25 s per address above 1, so among stations switched on together the lowest address leads. A station that hears a lead joins it; when two networks meet, the one with the lower lead address wins.

wavelink/tdma.py · the timing constantsTICK_S = 0.00025                 # unit of the slot plan
GUARD_S = 0.0005                 # gap between slots
IDLE_MS = 15                     # a slot whose owner has nothing (much) to send
DATA_MS = 100                    # ... and while it has data queued (a whole number of frames)
PLAN_AHEAD_S = 1.0               # a plan change takes effect this long after it is first announced
PLAN_AHEAD_CYCLES = 4            # ... and at least this many cycles later
LEAD_MISS = 2                    # lead headers missed before its successor takes over
EVICT_CYCLES = 6                 # a member silent this many cycles ...
EVICT_MIN_S = 1.5                # ... and this long loses its slot
LISTEN_S = 1.2                   # start-up: listen this long (+ 0.25 s per address) before leading
PROBE_BACKOFF_DB = 20            # a newcomer's first transmission: a probe on its own code, this much down

Timing in samples, not in PC time

A PC's clock and its buffers jitter by tens of milliseconds, far more than a 0.5 ms guard. So the slots are kept in sample counts of the radio. The TX and RX sides of one ANTSDR run from one sample clock, so a station's own burst always reaches its own receiver the same number of samples after it was written to the transmit stream. That constant is D, the TX → RX offset. It contains the TX buffers, the driver, the kernel buffers and the RX buffers, and none of them needs to be known separately.

wavelink/tdma.py · Tdma._calibrate_k(), measuring D from our own headerd = j - k                                # receive index of my burst - transmit sample I wrote it at
if self.D is None:
    self.D = d                           # first time: from the header's contents
    return
if abs(d - self.D) <= 4:                 # the same as before (± 4 samples): keep the median
    self._d_meas.append(d)
    self.D = sorted(self._d_meas)[len(self._d_meas) // 2]
    return
# a jump (TX underrun, lost RX buffer): believe it when two measurements agree; meanwhile a member
# sends only quiet probes (with D in doubt its bursts could land in the next or previous slot)
self._d_odd.append(d)
if len(self._d_odd) >= 2 and abs(self._d_odd[-1] - self._d_odd[-2]) <= 4:
    self.D = self._d_odd[-1]

Changing the plan safely

A station joins, leaves, or wants more or less airtime: the plan must change, and every station must switch on the same cycle. The lead announces each change in its header at least 1 s and 4 cycles before it takes effect, one change at a time, and every lead header repeats the plan in force. A station that last heard the plan in cycle L therefore knows every plan up to L + w (w = 10 cycles at 100 ms). Past that, it holds its slot instead of following a possibly stale plan into somebody else's. Why a full second: on the GNU Radio flowgraph a burst is built 0.2–0.6 s before it leaves the antenna, and a plan repeated by a relaying member is older again.

Slots grow on demand: each header says how much airtime its owner wants, a slot grows at the next plan change with 2 ms of headroom, and shrinks only after its owner has wanted at least 5 ms less for 1 s. A slot that should grow waits up to 1 s until every member has had a slot to say what it wants, so transfers that start together get their airtime in one plan change.

1.10 Relaying

Every slot header carries a link table: how well its station hears each other one (Es/N0 at full power). So every station knows who hears whom. When a destination doesn't hear us, or our messages to it keep timing out, and a station with relaying on hears both of us at 7 dB or more, the messages go through that station, one hop. The route goes back to direct once the direct path has been good (≥ 5 dB, no timeouts) for 5 s.

wavelink/tdma.py · Tdma.route(), choosing a relaydirect = self.hears(dst, self.addr)              # from dst's link table
good_direct = direct is not None and direct >= RELAY_DIRECT_DB and not self.mac.failing(dst)
if good_direct:
    return None                                   # direct
best, q = None, RELAY_MIN_DB                      # 7 dB on both hops
for rel, h in self.heard.items():
    if rel in (dst, self.addr) or not h.get("status", 0) & ST_RELAY:
        continue                                  # relaying switched off there
    a = self.hears(rel, self.addr)                # how the relay hears us
    b = self.hears(dst, rel)                      # how dst hears the relay
    if a is not None and b is not None and min(a, b) >= q:
        best, q = rel, min(a, b)                  # the strongest weakest hop wins
return best

Relaying also keeps a hidden station in time. A station that cannot hear the lead cannot know the cycle. Every member that hears the lead repeats the lead's plan in its own header while it hears a station that needs it (a newcomer, a station whose header says lead unheard, or one timing its slots by repeated plans), and passes on that station's join and airtime requests. This timing help works even with relaying switched off; switching relaying off only stops passing on messages.

Beacons are not relayed, so a relay also passes on who is at the other end: while some station it hears can't hear another one, its own beacon lists that station's name and picture tag ("v"). The far side then shows "Carol" with her picture, not "Node 3", and fetches the photo through the relay. A beacon stays valid JSON within 200 bytes: long names in a multi-byte script are shortened, never cut in the middle of a character. Chapter 9 shows a hidden station joining this way.

1.11 The application layer

node.py turns link-layer messages into chat. Each message envelope is crypto byte | meta length | meta JSON | body; the meta holds the kind (text, image, audio, file, game, rcpt, gc, prof, ctl), a uid, the send time, the group, file name and type. Text and compressible files are zlib-compressed; photos and Opus audio go as they are. History is kept in data/node<N>/history.jsonl with media beside it. The web server is the Python standard library: plain HTTP for actions and Server-Sent Events for live updates, so the UI loads nothing from the internet.

wavelink/crypto.py · AES-256-GCM with the addresses as associated datakey = hashlib.scrypt(passphrase.encode(), salt=b"WaveLink-chat", n=2 ** 14, r=8, p=1, dklen=32)
self.aead = AESGCM(key)
self.key_id = hashlib.sha256(key).hexdigest()[:8]     # shown in UI to compare keys

def seal(self, data: bytes, src: int, dst: int) -> bytes:
    nonce = os.urandom(12)                            # a fresh 96-bit nonce per message
    return bytes([SEALED]) + nonce + self.aead.encrypt(nonce, data, bytes([src, dst]))

Because (src, dst) is authenticated, a ciphertext replayed to another station fails. Beacons advertise the key id, and the UI warns when a peer uses a different key. Presence comes from every frame heard: with TD-CDMA that is a header from every station every cycle, so a station that has gone is noticed in 3 s.

2

Why TD-CDMA, and not CSMA, FDMA, TDMA, DS-CDMA or OFDMA

TD-CDMA takes one rule from TDMA (only one station transmits at a time) and keeps CDMA inside each slot (one Gold code per destination). Four facts about this hardware decided it: a station is deaf while it transmits, a burst leaves the antenna 0.2–0.6 s after it is built, all stations share one 4 MHz channel with CPU-bound receivers, and the lab has near, far and hidden stations.

1 · Deaf while transmitting

TX and RX antennas sit a few centimetres apart on the same frequency, so a station's own signal reaches its receiver about 25 dB above anyone else's. While it sends, it hears nothing else.

2 · Slow, jittery path to the antenna

The flowgraph gets a burst 120–450 ms before its slot, and libiio keeps about 82 ms of samples in its TX buffers. The PC cannot react to the channel in milliseconds, let alone microseconds.

3 · One channel, CPU-bound receivers

One ANTSDR per PC, one 4 MHz channel, and Python DSP: a receiving station already needs about 2.1 cores of a 2.8 GHz Xeon.

4 · Near, far and hidden stations

Stations can be 1 m or 10 m apart, and in another room a pair may not hear each other at all.

SchemeDeaf while sending0.2–0.6 s TX latencyNear-farHidden stationsSeveral destinations at oncePeak rate per linkBuilt here
CSMA/CApartly: no collision detectionfails: sensing is staleokcollisions (RTS/CTS costs round trips)nofullno, reasoned
FDMAok if the front end has the rangeokleakage and IQ imagesno helpno: one channel per sender¼ of the bandno, reasoned
TDMA, one codeokok with sample timingokneeds relaysno: one destination at a timefullno, reasoned
DS-CDMA alone (spread ALOHA)fails: 755–900 retransmissionsokneeds power controlunreachableyesfullyes: --mac aloha
OFDMAneeds schedulingneeds a central schedulerneeds power controlno helpyesshare of subcarriersno, reasoned
TD-CDMA (WaveLink)ok: nobody else is on the airok: slots in radio samplesnone: one transmitterone-hop relayyes: one code each~80 % of ALOHA'syes, the default

CSMA: listening before talking needs a fast radio

Carrier sense multiple access waits until the channel is quiet and then transmits. It works when the time from "the channel is free" to "my signal is on the air" is far shorter than a frame; Wi-Fi's slot time is 9 µs. Here a burst is handed to GNU Radio 120 to 450 ms before it should start, passes the code lanes and the Burst Combiner in 62–102 ms, and then sits in about 82 ms of TX buffers. A decision based on what the channel sounded like would be 0.2–0.6 s old by the time the burst leaves, and another station could have started in the meantime.

Sensing itself is also hard with spread signals. A WaveLink burst still decodes when each chip is 10 dB below the noise, so an energy detector cannot tell a busy channel from a quiet one; the receiver would have to despread every code just to sense. A half-duplex station cannot detect a collision while it sends, and hidden stations, which never hear each other, collide anyway. RTS/CTS fixes that in Wi-Fi at the cost of two extra exchanges per frame, and each exchange costs a 0.2–0.6 s round trip here.

FDMA: a channel each wastes the channel

Frequency division would give each of up to four stations a quarter of the 4 MHz. A link could then never use more than its quarter, even when the other three are idle, and the guard bands between sub-channels take more. Every receiver would need a channelizer and three demodulators running all the time, roughly three times today's receive CPU. Its own transmitter, 25 dB above everyone at its receiver, leaks into the neighbouring sub-channels and leaves an IQ image at the mirror frequency; on a cheap front end that needs filtering and guard bands, or the deafness comes back. Group messages need either a common channel or a copy per channel.

TDMA with a single code: we kept its rule, and added codes

WaveLink is a TDMA system at the level of who transmits when. What the codes add inside a slot:

  • Several destinations in one slot. Alice's slot can carry a photo to Bob on code 2 and a voice note to Carol on code 3 at the same time. With one code they would have to share the slot in time.
  • Addressing in the physical layer. A station despreads only its own code and code 0, so it never spends CPU demodulating traffic for others. With one code every receiver would decode every frame to read its dst.
  • Processing gain. 14.9 dB against noise and against other groups' signals in the shared 2.4 GHz lab band. The preamble detector works at about 4 dB symbol SNR, which is −11 dB per chip.
  • Safe join attempts. Two newcomers whose join requests collide in the join slot usually still separate by code phase, and the quiet probes on a station's own code, 20 dB down, disturb nobody.

The price is rate. Without spreading, 4 MHz could carry about 2 Msymbol/s instead of 64.5 ksymbol/s. But the Python receiver already needs about 2 cores at 64.5 ksymbol/s, so the bandwidth that spreading spends could not have been used for speed on these PCs anyway.

DS-CDMA on its own: our first design, and why it lost

The project started with spread ALOHA: every station transmits whenever it likes, on the receiver's code, and CDMA separates the simultaneous links. It is still there (--mac aloha), and where a station could receive while transmitting it is the fastest scheme: 294–321 kb/s together for four senders against 160–180 kb/s for TD-CDMA. On real radios three things go wrong:

  • A station that is transmitting misses everything sent to it. ALOHA needs an ACK gap after every ACK request and a half-duplex deferral, and still lost 755–900 frames per test to deafness.
  • The near-far problem: Alice talking to Carol right next to her drowns Bob's weak signal to Dave on another code, because despreading only suppresses her by about 15 dB. Transmit power control was built to fix this: Bob's 40 KB went from not delivered at all to 4.6–9.1 s. It works, but it costs the strong links speed.
  • Stations that cannot hear each other cannot talk, and a group message is one unicast per member.

OFDMA: powerful, but not on these radios and this CPU

OFDMA gives each user a set of subcarriers. On the uplink every user's symbols must arrive within the cyclic prefix of each other, and every user's carrier offset must be corrected to a small fraction of the subcarrier spacing before the FFT, or the subcarriers interfere. Two ANTSDR crystals rated ±2 ppm can be about 10 kHz apart at 2.5 GHz, so each station would need closed-loop frequency and timing control from a central scheduler. OFDM also has a high peak-to-average power ratio (more DAC headroom), and IQ imbalance puts each subcarrier's image on its mirror subcarrier, which belongs to someone else.

OFDM's big advantage is resistance to multipath. With 0.5 µs chips and indoor delay spreads of tens of nanoseconds, the lab channel stays within one chip, so that advantage buys little here. Building a multi-user OFDMA receiver in Python on top of everything else would have been a second project.

What TD-CDMA costs

One link alone gets about 80 % of ALOHA's speed (190 against 236 kb/s for a 2 MB file between two stations), because every cycle also has the receiver's own slot, the join slot (11.5 ms) and the headers (5–15 ms each). Keeping slots aligned to the sample needs the TX → RX offset measurement, probes and the hold rule described in 1.9. In exchange it works on radios that go deaf while transmitting, it has no near-far problem, and it makes relaying possible.

3

Why relaying, and not a hub or a ring

In one lab room every station hears every other, so the best topology is no topology: everyone talks directly. Relaying adds one hop only for the pairs that cannot hear each other, chooses the relay by itself from the link tables, and can use any station. A hub would double the airtime of every message and stop the network when it fails; a ring would add up to three hops and break on any single failure.

Hub (star)RingWaveLink (direct + one-hop relay)
Hops for a message2 (1 to or from the hub)1 to 3 with four stations1; 2 only for a hidden pair
Airtime per message2× for almost every message1× to 3×1×; 2× only through a relay
One station failsThe hub: everything stopsThe ring is broken until it is rebuiltOnly its own traffic stops; another relay is chosen
LoadThe hub receives and resends everything (receiving costs ~2.1 cores)Every station forwards trafficA relay forwards only for hidden pairs
SetupPick a hub that hears everyoneFix an order that keeps neighbours in rangeNone: chosen from link tables, back to direct when the path recovers

Relaying could also be fully multi-hop routing. With at most four stations, one hop covers every arrangement where some station hears both ends, which is the realistic case for a lab and a neighbouring room. Multi-hop is listed under future improvements.

4

Why Gold codes

The receivers see other stations' bursts at arbitrary code phases, so the codes must stay nearly uncorrelated at every shift, not only when aligned. Gold codes of length 31 guarantee a cross-correlation of at most 9/31 (−10.7 dB) at any shift, give 33 codes from one generator pair, have sharp autocorrelation for finding the preamble, and keep the symbol rate at 64.5 ksymbol/s.

Code familyLengthCodes availableWorst cross-correlation, any shiftAutocorrelation sidelobesWorks unsynchronisedSymbol rate at 2 Mchip/s
Gold (WaveLink)31339/31 (−10.7 dB)≤ 9/31yes64.5 k/s
m-sequences31611/31 (−9.0 dB)1/31, idealtoo few codes64.5 k/s
Walsh-Hadamard32320 aligned, 32/32 shiftedup to 32/32no: needs chip sync and a scrambling code62.5 k/s
Kasami (small set)6389/63 (−16.9 dB)≤ 9/63yes31.7 k/s
Gold, longer63 · 12765 · 12917/63 · 17/127same boundyes31.7 · 15.7 k/s

Why not Walsh codes. They would remove the small interference between the codes of one transmitter inside a slot, where bursts do start on the same chip. But they need every burst chip-synchronous under one scrambling code, a spreading factor of 32 and new preambles, and the measured signal-to-interference between Gold codes from one transmitter is already 39.9, 29.4 and 25.3 dB with 1, 2 and 3 codes at once, above the 22.5 dB that uncoded 16-QAM needs. Across slots and stations, where timing is never perfect, Walsh codes would be worse.

Why not longer codes. 63 or 127 chips would add 3 or 6 dB of processing gain and more codes, but halve or quarter the bit rate at the same chip rate. With only one transmitter on the air at a time, the extra suppression isn't needed, and five codes (broadcast plus four stations) of the 33 are enough.

How they are made. Two m-sequences from a preferred pair of 5th-degree polynomials, x⁵ + x² + 1 and x⁵ + x⁴ + x³ + x² + 1, are added modulo 2 at each of the 31 relative shifts; with the two sequences themselves that gives 33 codes. They are sorted so that the balanced codes (one more −1 than +1) come first, so the five in use have the smallest DC component. Each code also gets its own 48-bit preamble pattern, chosen so that its differential correlation has low sidelobes and low correlation with every other code's pattern.

wavelink/codes.py · gold_codes()def gold_codes(n: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """All 2^n + 1 Gold codes of degree n as a (num_codes, N) array of +/-1."""
    a, b = preferred_pair(n)            # n = 5: taps (5, 2) and (5, 4, 3, 2)
    N = a.size                          # 31
    codes = [a, b] + [a ^ np.roll(b, -k) for k in range(N)]
    arr = np.array(codes, dtype=np.int8)
    # put balanced codes first so the low indices used by real stations have the smallest DC
    bal = np.abs(arr.astype(int).sum(axis=1) * 2 - N)
    order = np.argsort(bal, kind="stable")
    return (1 - 2 * arr[order]).astype(np.float32)
5

Why relaying and time slots were added

The first version shared the air with spread ALOHA. Measurements showed three problems that no amount of tuning fixed: stations deaf while sending, the near-far problem, and stations that cannot hear each other. Time slots fixed the first two and made the third fixable; relaying fixed the third.

  1. Version 1 · spread ALOHAEvery link on the air whenever it likes, separated by codes. With a station's own transmitter 25 dB above the others, four simultaneous transfers delivered only 53–58 kb/s together with 755–900 retransmissions, despite ACK gaps and half-duplex deferral. A near pair drowned a far station unless transmit power control turned the near link down. A group message went as one copy per member. Stations out of each other's range could not talk.
  2. Version 2 · time slotsOne transmitter at a time, so nobody misses a frame because they are sending, and there is no near-far problem left. ACKs moved into the slot headers (no ACK frames, no pauses). A group message became one broadcast that every member acknowledges. The receiver searches only where slots start, which cut its CPU by more than half. Four simultaneous transfers: 173–181 kb/s together, about three times version 1.
  3. Version 3 · relayingSlots made it possible: every header already carries a link table, so every station knows who hears whom, and a relay forwards in its own slot without disturbing anyone. A hidden pair went from unreachable to 45–51 kb/s through a relay. The same headers let members repeat the lead's plan, so a station that cannot hear the lead still keeps time.
  4. Hardening on GNU RadioRunning the real flowgraph with emulated ANTSDRs exposed nine bugs, most of them in timing, all fixed: plan changes now wait 1 s (not 0.5 s) because a relayed plan can be 0.2–0.6 s old; newcomers probe before joining; a station that underran probes until it has measured its timing again; slots grow together. After the fixes 11 of 12 GNU Radio edge-case scenarios pass; the twelfth is real time on a 2-core PC (chapter 11).
6

How the two games are implemented

The game center runs two games for 2–4 stations over the same radio interface as the chat. UNO is turn-based, so the host's station decides everything and sends each player reliable, private views. The race is real time, so every station drives its own car and broadcasts its state once per cycle as an unacknowledged datagram in its own slot, and the others predict the car between updates.

6.1 Rooms, presence and hosts

A player picks opponents on a game's poster and presses Invite. Invitations, answers, the lobby, the start and the end travel as gc messages: reliable, sent at high priority so they overtake chat and file traffic, and not stored in the chat history (games/hub.py). With TD-CDMA a station whose slot header hasn't been heard for 3 s is away for up to 60 s: UNO pauses for everybody with a countdown, and the race keeps the car on the track as a frozen ghost. Heard again in time, the player carries on; later, the seat is dropped and the player is told the game went on.

If the host goes off the air, the next player in seat order takes over the room. Every takeover raises the room's host number, which every view and room message carries, so an old host that lost the connection and doesn't know yet recognises its claims as older and steps down. A chat panel and the radio dashboard open over a running game; keys typed in the panel never reach the game.

6.2 UNO: the host's station is the referee

  • Rules: 7 cards each; match colour or number/symbol, or play a Wild. Skip, Reverse (a Skip with two players), Draw Two, Wild, and Wild Draw Four only when you hold no card of the current colour (the host checks it, so there is no challenge). Draw one card instead of playing, then play or keep it. Call UNO with your second-to-last card; until the next player acts anyone can catch an uncalled UNO for a 2-card penalty. The winner scores the cards left in the other hands (numbers at face value, action cards 20, wilds 50).
  • Turn timer: 30 s, then the host plays the timeout for that player (draw and pass, keep a drawn card, or pick a colour).
  • On the air: game messages are high priority. On the GNU Radio flowgraph the code lanes are first-in first-out, so a view can wait behind a window of file frames (up to 0.6 s); if the player's next view is ready by then, the host withdraws the old one and sends one view carrying the events of both.
  • Host handover: every view also carries a copy of the whole table, kept in the station and never shown in the browser, so the next host can carry on.
  • Measured: a move reached every screen in a median 0.16 s with 2 stations, 0.22–0.24 s with 3 and 0.40 s with 4 (numpy simulator). Over the real flowgraph with emulated ANTSDRs, 16 of 16 moves reached both other players.
wavelink/games/uno.py · what a player may know, and a checked movedef view(self, seat: int) -> dict:
    """Everything seat may know: its own hand, the others' card counts, the table."""
    return dict(seat=seat, n=self.n, hand=sorted(self.hands[seat]), counts=[len(h) for h in self.hands],
                top=self.top, color=self.color, dir=self.direction, turn=self.turn, phase=self.phase,
                drawn=self.drawn if seat == self.turn else None, legal=self.legal_cards(seat), ...)

def play(self, seat: int, cid: int, color: int | None = None, uno: bool = False) -> dict:
    self._check_turn(seat, ("play", "drawn"))
    if cid not in self.hands[seat]:
        raise UnoError("You don't have that card")
    if not self.playable(cid, seat):
        if v == WILD4:
            raise UnoError(f"Wild Draw Four only when you have no {COLORS[self.color]} card")
        ...

6.3 Gold Code GP: every station drives its own car

  • The track is generated from the room's seed: a closed spline through 9–12 random points, redrawn if a corner is too tight or two parts come too close. Every station builds the same track and city without sending them.
  • The packet (games/race.py) is 28 bytes: room, seat, sequence, time since the green light, position, heading, velocity, yaw rate, distance raced, flags and the item; plus 13 bytes per event. With one event the frame is 52 bytes, 7.9 ms at QPSK ½.
  • Events (missile fired, mine dropped, EMP, hit, finish) ride in the state packets and are repeated in the next 4 packets, so one lost packet loses nothing; receivers drop the copies.
  • Hits are decided by the victim's station, which knows exactly where its car was: it simulates an incoming missile against its own position, checks mines as it drives over them, and checks an EMP against where it was when the EMP went off (it keeps 2 s of its positions). Then it broadcasts a hit.
  • Clocks: the countdown and finish times use the host's clock. Each player measures its offset with datagram pings and keeps the sample with the shortest round trip; the race starts only when everyone is synchronised.
  • A page reload doesn't lose the car: the station keeps the last state it was posted, with the lap start, best lap and event counter, and the reloaded page opens straight into the race and carries on from there. Event ids count as seen for 10 s only, so ids that wrap at 256 or restart after a reload still get through.
  • Update rate: one state per car per cycle, so 10 a second while nobody sends a file (100 ms cycle), 4.7 at 213 ms and 2.4 at 415 ms. Over the real flowgraph with emulated ANTSDRs each car's state reached both other players in 60–98 % of cycles.

Dead reckoning. Between updates the other cars are drawn where their last state says they are now. The prediction runs in track coordinates (distance along the centre line and offset across it): a car that was following the track keeps following it at its speed for up to 1.5 s, its sideways drift fades, and its offset is clamped to the rails, so a remote car is never drawn through a wall. When a new state disagrees with the prediction, the difference is blended out over 0.16 s. Compare it with plain straight-line extrapolation:

The chat also has a two-player tic-tac-toe, sent as ordinary game messages, which predates the game center.

7

Special features

Beyond the brief's core and its three bonus items (encryption, priority, dashboard), these are built and tested:

On the radio

5G NR LDPC with adaptive rate

Rates ½ to ⅔ to ⅚ or uncoded, BPSK to 16-QAM, chosen per link and per frame from the receiver's SNR reports. Up to 4.8 times the goodput of an uncoded link at 14 dB.

ldpc.py · nr_bg1.py · mac.py

TD-CDMA with multi-code slots

One slot per station; inside it, one code per destination at the same time. Slots sized on demand, joining, leaving, lead handover, duplicate-address warning.

tdma.py

One-hop relaying

Chosen automatically from the link tables, switchable live from the dashboard or --relay; relayed messages are marked "via Bob" at both ends, and the relay's beacon passes on the far station's name and picture.

tdma.py · route()

Group messages as one broadcast

Acknowledged by every member in its own header, with a tick count per member (2/3) and a fallback copy for members that miss it.

tdma.py · mac.py

Transmit power control

Every frame at the power its receiver needs (target 25.5 dB), closed loop through ACKs and beacons, with an outer loop for impairments the SNR estimate doesn't show.

mac.py

Encryption

AES-256-GCM, scrypt-derived key, a fresh nonce per message and the addresses as associated data; a key id in the beacons warns about mismatched keys.

crypto.py

On the screen

Radio dashboard

Constellation, spectrum, Es/N0, chip SNR, CFO, counters, queues, the links table with power per link, the slot plan, TX → RX offset D, clock drift in ppm, late bursts, the relay switch and routes, group ACKs per member.

Media at a chosen quality

A sheet shows every version's size and time on air before sending: photos at 480, 640, 1280 px or the original; voice notes and audio re-encoded to Opus 12 or 24 kb/s with a WebM muxer written for the app. A camera with live preview.

Messages in the order they were sent

Each station estimates every other station's clock offset; a photo overtaken on the air by a later text slides up into its place and is marked "⏱ 18 s late".

Cancel from either end

The sender's ✕ withdraws the transfer and tells the receiver; the receiver's ✕ tells the sender to stop ("cancelled by Bob").

Profiles over the air

Names and a picture tag in every beacon; a station that sees a new photo hash asks for the photo once, so each photo crosses the air once per pair.

Looks and sound

Eight palettes or a custom colour, light and dark, CSS wallpapers or a photo in a crop/rotate/adjust editor, an emoji palette of 1,167 emoji, synthesised sound effects and four built-in music loops, all working offline.

For testing without hardware

Numpy channel simulator

Up to four stations with per-link gain, delay, carrier offset, AWGN, clock error, cut links and self-leak: python3 -m wavelink sim.

GNU Radio simulation

grc/cdma_phy_sim.grc: three station PHYs through a stock Channel Model, the same chain as on hardware.

Fake ANTSDRs

The real app and the unchanged flowgraph per station, with the two ANTSDR blocks emulated (libiio buffers, underruns, lost RX buffers, clipping) and the air between them simulated.

8

Edge cases and how they are handled

Every case below has an automated test. "Numpy" is the simulator suite (tests/test_edge.py: 93 of 93 checks in the latest run, after the relay and short-message fixes of this review; in the run before them 91 of 92, and the one miss, a single message in the clock-drift scenario, did not come back in four reruns); "GNU Radio" is the real flowgraph with emulated ANTSDRs (tests/test_fake_antsdr.py, 55 of 58 checks, the air at 0.4× real time). Both record every moment two stations transmit at once where a third hears both; inside a formed network that never happened.

Network formation

Stations switched on one by one, in any order

HandlingA starting station listens 1.2 s plus 0.25 s per address above 1. If it hears a lead it joins; otherwise it leads. The incumbent keeps leading when later stations arrive.

EvidenceNumpy: 3, then 1, then 2 gave one network led by 3. GNU Radio: the same, pass.

Network formation

All stations switched on at the same moment

HandlingThe lowest address listens shortest, so station 1 starts leading first and the others hear its header and join.

EvidenceNumpy: 4 stations, one network led by 1 after 2.3 s. GNU Radio: 3 radios, after 4.8 s of air, pass.

Network formation

Two separate networks come into range

HandlingThe network whose lead has the lower address wins; the other lead yields and its members join. A station that hears both networks joins them.

EvidenceGNU Radio: two lone stations merged under the lower address in 1.5 s, pass. See chapter 11 for the brief overlap during a merge, and chapter 9 to watch a merge.

Network formation

Two newcomers at the same moment

HandlingJoin requests start at a random point in the first 4 ms of the join slot, in a random half of the cycles. If two still collide, their code phases usually separate them.

EvidenceNumpy: both had a slot after 1.2 s, pass.

Network formation

Two radios set to the same address

HandlingEvery header carries a random 16-bit nonce. Two nonces that keep alternating under one address are announced in the headers, and the stations concerned show "Another station is using address N". A nonce that changes once is a restart, not a duplicate.

EvidenceNumpy and GNU Radio: the warning appeared within seconds, pass; a lead restarted within 10 s is not flagged.

Joining and leaving

A station joins and the lead leaves during a transfer

HandlingPlan changes go one at a time, each announced at least 1 s and 4 cycles ahead, and the transfer keeps its slot through both.

EvidenceNumpy: delivered intact at 156 kb/s, no late burst, no overlap, pass.

Joining and leaving

The lead's PC dies mid-transfer

HandlingAfter 2 missed lead headers the next lowest address takes over, if it still hears other stations and none of them heard the lead in the last 3 cycles. Cycle numbers and timing carry on. The old lead, back, joins as a member.

EvidenceNumpy: takeover after 0.58 s, transfer at 177 kb/s. GNU Radio (kill -9): 0.71 s, transfer intact at 150 kb/s, only the successor took over, pass.

Joining and leaving

A station off the air for a moment, or for longer

HandlingA station keeps its slot until its headers have been missing for 6 cycles and 1.5 s; then the lead frees the slot in the next plan. Back on the air, it asks in every join slot.

EvidenceNumpy: 1 s kept, 2.5 s freed and back 0.12 s after return. GNU Radio: 1 s kept, 3.5 s dropped after 3.0 s and back 1.4 s after return, pass.

Joining and leaving

A station misses every plan-change announcement

HandlingThe hold rule: past the cycles it knows the plan for, it holds its slot until it hears the plan in force, instead of transmitting by a stale plan.

EvidenceNumpy: 93 headers dropped over 5 plan changes, never overlapped, everything delivered, pass.

Joining and leaving

A station stops hearing the lead, the others still do

HandlingIt marks its header lead unheard; members repeat the lead's plan for it; nobody takes over, because the others still hear the lead.

EvidenceNumpy, relaying on and off: its transfer went on at 165 kb/s, no takeover, pass.

Timing

Sample clocks 25 ppm apart

HandlingEvery lead header re-anchors the followers, which also measure their clock against the lead's to bridge missed headers. D is a property of one radio and doesn't drift.

EvidenceNumpy: every message delivered (299 of 299 over 10 min), D moved 0 samples, each follower's drift within 0.1 ppm of the true −50 / −15. GNU Radio: 80 of 80, −50.0 / −15.0 ppm, pass.

Timing

TX underruns and lost RX buffers

HandlingA slip moves D. The new value is believed once two measurements agree; meanwhile the member sends only quiet probes (at most 4 slots) and its receiver searches everywhere for 1.5 s.

EvidenceGNU Radio, 5 injected slips: every D moved by exactly what its streams slipped, both transfers intact. Numpy, 6 slips: delivered, pass.

Timing

A station that cannot hear itself

HandlingEvery header lists, for each station heard, how many samples off its header arrived. A station whose own headers don't come back moves D by 0.7 × the median report.

EvidenceNumpy: the deaf station kept its timing from the reports and delivered at 82 kb/s, pass.

Timing

A newcomer that doesn't know its own D yet

HandlingIts first guess on the flowgraph was 7–28 ms short, enough to land a join request on the lead's header. It sends quiet probes on its own code, 20 dB down, until it hears one and knows D.

EvidenceGNU Radio: after the fix no join request overlapped a slot in any test, pass.

Timing

A PC that falls behind

HandlingThe despreader queues up to 3 s; dropped chunks keep the sample count right and don't count as timing faults. Bursts are handed over earlier (120–450 ms) after a late one, and a burst that misses its chip is dropped, never sent into another slot.

EvidenceGNU Radio in real time on 2 cores: overloaded and the network didn't form, but no burst was late and none overlapped. The scenario itself fails (chapter 11).

Joining and leaving

A station reached only through a relay

HandlingIt shows as online "via Bob". Bob's beacon passes on its name and picture tag; the photo is fetched through Bob. Long names in multi-byte scripts are shortened so a beacon stays valid JSON within 200 bytes.

EvidenceNumpy, 1 and 3 out of range: names and picture arrive through 2; 32-character Japanese and Kannada names give beacons of 136–200 bytes, all valid; back in range, the station's own beacon wins, pass.

Channel and range

Low SNR

HandlingThe Golay header decodes down to ~1 dB and QPSK ½ is the floor. A takeover needs the others to confirm the lead is gone, so lost lead headers don't cause false takeovers.

EvidenceNumpy at 5 dB: the network forms, messages delivered (14 retransmissions), 0 takeovers. GNU Radio at 10 dB: a file at 53 kb/s, 0 takeovers, pass.

Channel and range

Bursty interference, 3 dB below the signal

HandlingLDPC and ARQ absorb the hits; the rate follows the latest SNR reports while the power follows the path.

EvidenceNumpy, 25 % of the time: 122 and 136 kb/s, 0 retransmissions. GNU Radio, 20 %: 111 kb/s, pass.

Channel and range

Near-far without power control

HandlingOne transmitter on the air at a time, so a near station cannot drown a far one.

EvidenceNumpy: the far station got 67 kb/s with 0 retransmissions (spread ALOHA: 43 kb/s, 16 retransmissions), pass.

Channel and range

A hidden station

HandlingOne-hop relaying through a station that hears both, plus plan repetition so the hidden station keeps time.

EvidenceGNU Radio: 40 KB from 1 to 3 through 2 at 43 kb/s, intact, and a message back, pass.

Channel and range

Relaying switched off during a relayed transfer

HandlingThe relay stops passing messages on, so the transfer waits; timing is still repeated, so the network stays one. Frames lost on the way are resent once the route is back.

EvidenceNumpy: 0 % while off, completed after relaying came back on, one network throughout, pass.

Channel and range

A hidden station with relaying off everywhere

HandlingMembers still repeat the plan (timing only), so the outer stations share one network and each reaches the middle station.

EvidenceNumpy: Carol and Alice both sent to Bob at 103 and 98 kb/s, no overlap, pass.

Traffic

Every station sending at once

HandlingEqual slots for everyone with data; a growing slot waits for the others' wishes so all slots grow in one plan change.

EvidenceNumpy, 4 senders: 146–156 kb/s together; slowest over fastest 0.53–0.62 in the quick run, 0.71–0.74 in the full run, pass.

Traffic

A group message with a member out of range, who then leaves

HandlingOne broadcast plus a relayed copy for the far member; ticks from both. When the member is gone, the next group message is given up for it instead of held.

EvidenceNumpy: relayed copy delivered and filed in the group, the gone member given up, pass.

Traffic

An urgent text during a large file

HandlingEach code in a slot serves control, urgent, normal and bulk messages in that order.

Evidencetests/test_link.py priority checks, pass.

Traffic

A transfer cancelled from either end; a message overtaken on the air

Handlingctl cancel and stop messages drop the partial message on both sides. Messages are placed by send time, converted to this station's clock, and marked late if they arrive more than 4 s after sending.

Evidencetests/test_features.py and the browser checks in tests/ui_features.py, pass.

Games

A racer leaves and comes back, another leaves for good

HandlingNo header for 3 s: away, shown as a frozen ghost while the race goes on. Back within 60 s: races on. Later: dropped on every station.

EvidenceNumpy, 4 players: all 7 checks, pass.

Games

A race page reloaded mid-race

HandlingThe station keeps the car's last posted state (position, speed, distance raced, lap start, best lap, item, event counter); the reloaded page opens straight into the race and the car carries on from there, laps and pickup kept.

EvidenceBrowser test, 3 stations: reloaded at 8,624 px raced, resumed at 8,624 px; the race finished normally, pass.

Games

UNO: a player away, the host away, a player back too late

HandlingThe game pauses for everybody with a countdown and the hand is kept. With the host away, the next seat hosts from the table copy in its view; the old host plays on under the new one. After the grace period the seat is dropped and the player is told the game went on.

EvidenceNumpy: all 10 checks, pass.

9

Network playground: stations joining, leaving and moving

This simulation runs the time-slot rules of tdma.py, cycle by cycle, for the four stations on a floor plan of two labs. Switch stations on and off, unplug an antenna, drag a station away or behind the wall, start a file transfer or an interference burst, and watch what every station decides, and when. The scenario buttons replay the edge cases of chapter 8. The log says what happened and which rule caused it.

What the playground models

The rules and their constants are the ones in the code. The radio channel is the part that is made up: on the lab floor real links depend on antennas, people and furniture.

What you seeRuleIn the code
A station listens before it leads1.2 s + 0.25 s × (address − 1); a station that hears a header carrying the plan joins instead_reset, LISTEN_S, LISTEN_STEP_S
A lone lead's header in every 4th cycleAlone and with nothing to send, the lead transmits in cycles 4, 8, 12 … and listens in the others, so a second network can be heard_service_lead
Probe, then join requestsA newcomer first sends its header on its own code, 20 dB down, to measure its TX → RX offset D; then a join request in the join slot, in about half the cycles (every cycle after it was dropped)_send_join, PROBE_BACKOFF_DB
Plans announced aheadA plan change takes effect at least 4 cycles and 1 s after it is first announced; the lead makes one change at a timeplan_window(), PLAN_AHEAD_S, PLAN_AHEAD_CYCLES
Slot sizes15 ms with nothing queued, about 100 ms with data; a cycle under 100 ms gets the spare time added to its slots; growth waits 0.3 s for the others' wishes, a slot shrinks after 1 s_lead_plan_update, _settle, IDLE_MS, DATA_MS, MIN_CYCLE_MS, GATHER_S, SHRINK_S
A slot heldA member sends in cycle n only if it heard the plan that covers cycle n; otherwise it stays silent rather than risk a stale plan_service_follower
A slot freedA member silent for at least 1.5 s and 6 cycles loses its slot (with a grace period before its first slot)EVICT_MIN_S, EVICT_CYCLES
The lead's successor takes overAfter 2 missed lead headers, plus 2 more per station ranked before it, if it hears someone else, nobody reports hearing the lead, and nobody ranked before it is still on the air_service_follower, _take_over, LEAD_MISS
A station starts overNo plan heard for 3 s: it listens again, and then joins or leadsLOST_S
Two networks meetThe lower address leads: a lead that hears a lower lead's plan, directly or repeated, gives up its network and joins_on_lead_header
A member repeats the planWhile it hears a newcomer, a lone lead with a higher address, or a station that says it can't hear the lead, a member puts the lead's plan in its own header; it also passes on that station's join request_relay_sync_needed
A file goes via a relayDirect below 5 dB (or not heard): through the station that hears both ends best, at 7 dB or more; back to direct after 5 s of a good direct linkroute(), RELAY_DIRECT_DB, RELAY_MIN_DB
Modulation per linkThe fastest entry of the ladder whose threshold the link clears: QPSK ½ at 5 dB … 16-QAM ⅚ at 14 dB, uncoded 16-QAM at 22.5 dBMCS_TABLE, mac._level
Power in the cardOne power per slot: what its weakest listener needs to reach 25.5 dB, at most 30 dB down; with more than two codes in the slot they share the power_slot_bo, pc_target_db

Simplified on purpose

Link Es/N0 = 52 dB − TX attenuation − 26·log10(distance in m) − 15 dB per wall, the same in both directions. A header is decoded with a probability that rises from 19 % at 4 dB to 99 % at 6 dB (the preamble detector is reliable from about 4 dB, the QPSK ½ header needs about 5 dB); a data frame decodes in the same way around its modulation's threshold. Files move at 85 % of the raw rate while their station is sending, ACKs are not drawn, the header is 8 ms and the join slot 11.5 ms. Sample timing (D, clock drift, receive indices) is not simulated; chapter 1.9 and the edge cases cover it.

Things to try.

  • In Switch on one by one, step through Bob's arrival with Step one cycle: his probe and join request appear in the join slot, Alice announces the next plan, and his slot appears in the bar only when that plan takes effect, a second later.
  • With the wall unchecked, send Carol a file and drag her slowly to the far corner: the link label drops, the line changes colour, and the log shows each step down of the modulation. Past about 27 m her headers stop arriving; 1.5 s later her slot is freed, and 3 s later she starts over and leads a network of her own.
  • Drag her back: Alice's lower address wins, Carol gives up her network and joins Alice's again.
  • Raise the TX attenuation to 25 dB with the four stations spread out: some pairs stop hearing each other, routes go through relays, and members start repeating the plan for the stations that can't hear the lead.
  • Switch off the lead while a file is on its way between the others; then switch it on again: it comes back as a member.
10

Running it, testing it, demonstrating it

10.1 Install and bring-up

Each lab PC needs Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04 with GNU Radio 3.10 or later, which brings grcc and gr-iio (the PlutoSDR blocks the ANTSDR uses). Nothing else is needed for the chat; the web server is the Python standard library and the UI loads nothing from the internet. cryptography is only needed for --key.

bash · on every PCsudo apt install gnuradio python3-numpy      # grcc and gr-iio come with it
pip install cryptography                     # only for --key (encryption)
iio_info -u ip:192.168.1.10                  # 1. the PC reaches its ANTSDR
python3 -m wavelink selftest --radio loopback   # 2. GNU Radio works
grcc -o build/grc grc/cdma_phy.grc           # 3. the flowgraph compiles (the app does this at every start)
  • ANTSDR firmware. The flowgraph uses the Pluto-compatible (libiio) firmware: boot DIP switch to QSPI, default address ip:192.168.1.10, the PC's Ethernet port on 192.168.1.x. Several ANTSDRs on one switch need different addresses (fw_setenv ipaddr_eth 192.168.1.11 in the device shell, then reboot); one cable per PC can keep .10 everywhere.
  • Antennas. TX1 and RX1, separate 2.4 GHz-band antennas, a few centimetres apart or more. A station must hear its own header to measure D; one that can't is steered by the others' timing reports.
  • UHD firmware (SD boot, MicroPhase's antsdr_uhd) only works with the numpy PHY (--phy numpy --radio uhd), unless the two PlutoSDR blocks of the .grc are swapped for UHD blocks.

10.2 Commands

python3 -m wavelink rx --id 2
python3 -m wavelink tx --id 1 --to 2 --text "Hello"

The mid-evaluation simplex link: the transmitter repeats a text every second on node 2's code; the receiver prints each frame with its modulation, symbol SNR, carrier offset and preamble metric. BPSK with LDPC ½ by default (--mcs bpsk, --mcs 16qam-3/4 …). Its bursts are compatible with the flowgraph PHY.

python3 -m wavelink run --id 1 --name Alice --key "secret"

One station: compiles grc/cdma_phy.grc with grcc, starts it, attaches the link layer to its MAC → PHY and PHY → MAC blocks and serves the UI on http://localhost:8080. IDs 1–4, one per station.

python3 -m wavelink sim --nodes 4
python3 -m wavelink sim --nodes 3 --cut 1:3

The numpy channel simulator: up to four stations in one process on ports 8081–8084, with per-link gain, delay, carrier offset and AWGN; --cut, --link-gain 1:3=24, --ppm 2=40, --ebn0, --self-leak, --mac aloha.

python3 -m wavelink grc-sim

Three copies of the station PHY in grc/cdma_phy_sim.grc, summed through a stock Channel Model (--noise, --cfo), at 1 MS/s because the three share one Python process.

python3 -m wavelink fake-air
python3 -m wavelink run --id 1 --uri fake: --port 8081

Fake ANTSDRs: each station is the real app on the unchanged flowgraph, with the two ANTSDR blocks emulated (libiio buffers, underruns, lost RX buffers, clipping) and the air between them in fake-air (--cut, --ppm, --speed 0.5 for a slow PC, a JSON control port for live faults).

python3 -m wavelink selftest --radio loopback

Frames to itself through GNU Radio, as a first check of an install.

The flags of run (most also work with sim):

FlagDefaultEffect
--id, --name—Address 1–4 (= the station's Gold code) and the display name; a name changed in the UI wins.
--keynoneAES-256-GCM with a key from scrypt; every station needs the same passphrase, and a mismatch is shown in the UI.
--uriip:192.168.1.10The ANTSDR's libiio address; fake: for the fake radios.
--tx-atten, --rx-gain, --freq10 dB, 40 dB, 2.5 GHzThe flowgraph's radio parameters; raise the gain for distance, lower it if the spectrum clips; every station on the same carrier.
--mactdcdmaaloha runs the earlier spread ALOHA (every station the same).
--relayonPass on messages for stations that can't hear each other; also a switch on the dashboard.
--mod, --fecauto, autoRestrict the modulation (bpsk, qpsk, 16qam) or the code rate (off, 1/2 … 5/6); together they pin one entry.
--power-control, --pc-targeton, 25.5 dBTransmit power control and the Es/N0 it aims at.
--tx-buffer65536ANTSDR TX buffer in samples (16 ms); raise it if TX underruns climb.
--ack-gap, --hd-defer0.15 s, 0.25 sSpread ALOHA only: the pause after an ACK request, and the hold while a burst for us is arriving.
--host, --portlocalhost, 8080--host 0.0.0.0 lets other PCs open the UI (the microphone then needs localhost).
--grc, --phy numpygrc/cdma_phy.grcRun an edited copy of the flowgraph, or the fallback PHY without the .grc (it alone takes --radio uhd, --profile, --rate, --sps, --gold).

10.3 The GNU Radio Companion files

FileWhat it is
grc/cdma_phy.grcThe station's PHY on an ANTSDR (chapter 1.2). Parameters: node ID, ANTSDR URI, carrier, RX gain, TX attenuation, TX buffer. Used by run.
grc/cdma_phy_sim.grcThree copies of that PHY (nodes 1–3) joined by a Channel Model with noise and carrier-offset variables. Used by grc-sim.
grc/cdma_phy_concept.grcDS-CDMA from stock blocks only, with GUI plots: two users on Gold codes 1 and 2 summed with noise, then despread with the right and the wrong code. It shows processing gain live in the viva (F6); the app doesn't use it.

At every start grc_phy.py runs grcc on the file (so the last saved edit is what runs), imports the generated top block with the command-line values for its Parameter blocks, finds the Embedded Python blocks by node ID, attaches the link layer, reads the dashboard data from the CDMA Despreader and the Burst Combiner, and starts it. In GNU Radio Companion you can change the variables, add QT GUI sinks for measurements or swap the radio blocks; keep the seven Embedded Python blocks, the code/mod PDU routing between them and the constellations' point order (the Framer's Gray mapping). Pressing F6 in GRC runs the PHY on its own: PHY → MAC then prints received frames, a handy radio check. tools/make_grc.py regenerates all three files from tools/epy/ (overwriting edits made in GRC), and tools/render_grc.py draws a .grc's layout without GNU Radio.

10.4 The test suites

SuiteWhat it checksLatest result
